name: Eisenhower matrix
attribution: Popularised by Stephen Covey (1989), after a remark attributed to Dwight D. Eisenhower

claims.claim: Placing items on a spatial layout defined by two explicit dimensions makes their relative standing on both dimensions easier to judge and compare than a list or table does.
People prefer tasks framed as urgent (short completion windows) over important tasks with objectively larger payoffs. Separating urgency from importance should therefore counter that bias.
Items placed inside the same bounded region are perceived as belonging together, even against other grouping cues, so labelled zones make category membership readable at a glance.
claims.construct: the Gestalt principle of common region (perceptual grouping)

grounding.helps: when urgent-looking tasks keep crowding out important ones; people pick spuriously urgent tasks over better-paying ones, a small but replicated effect, though the grid as a fix and its four actions are untested craft
grounding.backfires: when urgency is rated from how pressing a task feels rather than from its real deadline, since spurious urgency is exactly what pulls choices, or when an axis does not discriminate and everything crowds one quadrant
